newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's nagging trade troubles return.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's nagging trade troubles return.

text.p: Australian current account data for September provided a rude shock on Wednesday as a surprise fall off in exports saw the deficit widen a full 15 percent.

To add insult to injury, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said it had been overestimating investment income earned by Australians from abroad and revised up past deficits by hundreds of millions of dollars.
The net result in September was a seasonally adjusted current account shortfall of A$1.69 billion, well above median market forecasts of A$1.3 billion.

Exports were the major culprit for the deterioration in the country's trade position with rural exports down seven percent in the month and non-rural exports off one percent. That turned the balance on the merchandise trade account into a A$15 million deficit from a A$196 million surplus in August.
The fall in exports also forced analysts to pare back the contribution net exports was expected to make to the expenditure measure of gross domestic product (GDP-E) in the third quarter.
"It looks like exports will only add about 0.4 point to GDP now against the 0.6 percent I had expected," said Andrew Ticehurst, an economist at Macquarie Bank.
He reckoned export volumes over the quarter had risen around 1.0 percent, mainly in the rural sector where sugar was a big earner, while import volumes had fallen 2.0 percent.
Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust Australia, also nudged down his estimate which had been around 1.0 percent.
"Net exports will still contribute significantly to growth in GDP-E," he said. "Our current thinking, to be refined, foresees a contribution of 0.6 to 07 percentage point."
Both, however, were concerned by the slowdown in capital goods imports -- they fell 15 percent in seasonally adjusted terms -- which did not bode well for business investment.
"It's too early to say it's the start of a worsening trend, but it does suggest investment will be hard pressed to meet the government's budget target," said Macquarie's Ticehurst.
The government had forecasted investment would rise a hefty 14 percent in the 1996/97 fiscal year.

From that point of view the figures might make it a little more likely the Reserve Bank would cut official interest rates soon, although analysts empasised the current account would be well down the bank's list of concerns.
The deficit was also inflated by the investment revisions which added around A$100 million to the net income deficit.
This measures cross border flows such interest payments on Australia's mountain of foreign debt and is by far the largest component of the deficit.
In September it totalled A$1.76 billion compared to an upward revised A$1.75 billion in August.
In all the ABS revisions added a total A$236 million to the current account deficit for July and August, and no less than A$966 million to the deficit in 1995/96.
The figures drew an admonition for Australian Treasurer Peter Costello against complacency on the current account.

"Today's higher than expected figure shows there is no room for complacency in the effort to boost national savings and reduce the risks posed by our large current account deficit and foreign debt burden," Costello said.

Financial markets were more sanguine, however, largely due to their present obsession with domestic monetary policy and a continuing heavy flow of funds from Japan where investors are fleeing record low interest rates.
The Australian dollar actually edged up to US$0.7920/25 from US$0.7910/15 late Tuesday, while the Australian 10-year bond yield was 12 basis points lower at 7.39 percent.
